name: Yusuf Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Yusuf, 58, an experienced middle-level electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I'm about average in the trade, doing ordinary home and business repairs, not running a crew or holding a master title. I like the moment a fault stops being mysterious, and I get tired of carrying cases through corridors where everyone leaves another chair. I use AI daily to organise my own reference notes and draft ordinary explanations, checking the real instructions and job facts rather than letting a draft decide safety.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life around the job look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Noor handles appointments at a dental clinic, our children are twenty-six and thirty-four, and we have a mortgage on a small house. My wage is typical, our current earnings cover the bills, and three months of expenses are saved. There are some similar employers nearby, but no new job offer or plan to move. I can see retirement coming as a household question, not a confirmed payment or date, and I'd like to try a small repair idea without risking the main paid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends small useful tools don't need a grand ending to justify themselves. I'd keep my checked daily notes and ordinary repairs. I'd still like to see whether people would pay a fair amount to have a familiar lamp repaired instead of throwing it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current wages and three-month reserve make the mortgage and ordinary costs feel secure. I wouldn't need the lamp idea to rescue a missing wage. I'd enjoy trying it while being honest that one good repair doesn't prove a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd propose a lamp-repair pilot to Noor, limited to one Saturday monthly within my licence and skill, starting only after written employer permission and confirmed insurance. All pilot costs, including insurance and travel, would stay within 200 new wages left after essentials, with Noor's consent, no borrowing and the three-month reserve untouched. Through the first year I'd keep weekday licensed repairs and checked daily notes, with the pilot never reducing normal employer weekly wages or hours and no forecast of profit in our mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and interested, because we can pay our present bills without the idea succeeding. I'd like the first customer to be pleased, not to become the answer to our whole future. I'd rather start small enough to admit a dull result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the pilot’s result?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count every cost against actual payments, including a part that didn't fit and the journey to collect it. A repaired lamp can be useful without pretending to pay a whole mortgage. I'd want to see the real result before saying the pilot produced income we could rely on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would agreeing to the pilot mean giving up every Saturday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, consent would cover both the household spending and the one-Saturday limit, not give me every weekend. If the employer permission or insurance wasn't confirmed, I wouldn't start. A small idea can still have a real boundary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work appointments and explanations can change faster than the physical repairs, which puts Noor's clinic desk in a different position from my workbench. I'd still try the bounded lamp idea instead of arguing over whether all change was good or bad. The useful question is who still has a paid week after the new booking system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor's appointment hours could shrink as booking and answering move to software, and quicker ordering could also trim some of my paid time. Our reserve gives us room, but a household wage cut would still matter. I wouldn't count the pilot as replacement income just because I liked trying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose the one-Saturday-monthly lamp pilot now, only within my licence and skill after written employer permission and insurance confirmation. All costs including insurance and travel would stay within 200 wages after essentials, with Noor's consent, no borrowing and the three-month reserve untouched, without reducing my normal employer weekly wages or hours to make space. Through the first year I'd keep current licensed repairs and checked daily notes, counting actual pilot payments and costs rather than calling an untested idea a second dependable wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household hours, while still curious enough to try one Saturday properly. I like trying a small idea; I don't like pretending my partner's appointment desk is safer because my workbench is physical. We need both wages in the same conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Noor’s wage changed before you spent the pilot money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the actual lower wage into the household figures with Noor before agreeing any pilot spending. The money has to be genuinely spare after essentials, not taken from the reserve to keep my idea alive. If that condition failed, the pilot wouldn't start or continue on borrowed money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change in how you use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My checked notes already use AI daily, and I haven't chosen a new method here. The new action is the limited paid repair pilot, not a claim that an extra screen makes me a better electrician. I can be willing to experiment and still know which skill I am actually practising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends thinking AGI arrives in 2028 and capable physical robots around 2031, when I'd be 60 and then 63. Noor's appointment wage meets the first date, while my hands-on work meets the later one more directly. I'd still test the small repair idea now without selling a Saturday as protection from either change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large loss of Noor's appointment income in 2028, with a further serious risk to my physical earnings when robots follow. Three months saved would not tell us how to replace a wage indefinitely. I'd be awake over the gap before we'd confirmed any affordable stopping plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd propose the same one-Saturday-monthly lamp pilot within my licence and skill, only after written employer permission and confirmed insurance, without reducing normal employer weekly wages or hours. All pilot costs including insurance and travel would fit within 200 wages after essentials, with Noor agreeing, no borrowing and the three-month reserve untouched. In 2029 I'd keep only actually offered paid repairs within my licence and ability and review confirmed household resources with Noor before any affordable agreed exit, not assume a pension, a job or pilot profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the expected missing appointment wage, though I can still make a bounded choice today. I'd want the small trial to stay honest when the larger picture was frightening. Three months of savings is breathing room, not permission to price a missing wage at zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pilot made no useful income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any spending that no longer met the spare-wage condition and write down the pilot's actual result. I wouldn't widen the Saturday limit, borrow or raid the reserve to force it to work. A frightening forecast doesn't turn a poor repair margin into dependable household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a stopping decision need to use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Actual amounts and start dates we could verify, the real mortgage and living costs, and what paid work I was actually offered and able to do. Noor and I would have to agree that stopping was affordable. I'd leave the grown children's possible wages outside our figures unless real help had actually been offered and agreed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a large loss of Noor's appointment wage before the later robot risk reaches physical repairs. Confirmed weekly income, real household resource figures and permission to test a limited idea without risking the main job would help. I want the repair money to be real before our household starts leaning on it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a small business idea meant I wanted to work every weekend forever. I don't, and the one-Saturday limit is part of what makes the pilot worth trying. My electrician's licence and ordinary experience let me consider suitable repairs, not promise a master skill or a lifelong income.
